rv.q: Instead, it’s bright, generous, and forceful, and those currents carry the day.
“Jaja’s” is full of such treasurable moments, when the drama feels tightly woven with the comedy.

Bioh — who notes in the program that she’s been wearing braids since she was 4 — has composed a character-rich play, bubbling with personality and marking Bioh’s Broadway debut as an occasion worth toasting.
This is an ensemble piece, a collection of character studies, a bubbly slice of the uptown hair-braiding life.

“ ‘Jaja’s African Hair Braiding’ celebrates business owners like Jaja and the ladies who work for her. It’s also a portrait that illustrates everything it takes for Black women, especially immigrants, to survive in this country.

The show shines in its jovial moments, limps in its solemn ones, and ultimately flails in its hurried, harrowed conclusion — but still deserves to be crowned the theatrical event of the season for Black women.
Such is the case with Ms. Bioh’s warm and buoyant play, set in the Harlem hair salon that gives the comic drama its title.
Jaja’s African Hair Braiding, a delightful Broadway debut by Jocelyn Bioh, is an ode to that experience, to the women who make it so.

The result is a play that is equally affecting as it is hilarious, weaving together expertly delivered punchlines and physical gags alongside frank discussions on race, immigration, and a few jabs at the racist rhetoric espoused by then-President Donald Trump.
Indeed, Jaja’s words will echo in our ears when the play takes a final, very dramatic twist.
Under the sure hand of director Whitney White, Jaja's African Hair Braiding is an altogether terrific ensemble piece.
In Jaja’s African Hair Braiding, Bioh has done them all proud.
I enjoyed spending an afternoon with these characters so much that I want more time in their presence.
Jocelyn Bioh intertwines their tales, director Whitney White shapes the action into a tight thing of beauty and the ensemble work of the energetic cast is streaked with highlights.
Bioh makes it with uncommon eloquence.
Jocelyn Bioh whose career continues on an upper trajectory has a potential hit with Jaja’s African Hair Braiding which is both funny and serious, revealing and surprising.
The performers make the most of Bioh’s sharp eye for character and precise ear for dialogue that’s both spot-on and hilarious.
Bioh’s play is a celebration of that.
It's a passionate portrayal of Black womanhood in Harlem and all the diverse experiences that encompasses.

Even though “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” takes place entirely in the hair salon, as does “Steel Magnolias,” the play is a series of short skits, as is “The Women”; and like that Boothe Luce play, many of those scenes lack a good button.

And this leaves Jaja’s African Hair Braiding as insufficiently dramatic, though never less than amusing, as acted by the 10-member cast and directed by Whitney White, who apparently knows exactly what has a braiding outfit buzzing any and every day.
Jaja’s African Hair Braiding, Ghanian-American playwright Jocelyn Bioh’s contribution to the job site oeuvre, is a rich, funny and moving entertainment.
Jaja’s African Hair Braiding is truly a masterpiece.

Bea offers unsolicited advice, especially towards Aminata (Nana Mensah) and the status of her marriage with her philandering husband James. Despite all her flaws or because of them, she’s a wonderfully entertaining character.
You won’t mind spending a lot more time in Jaja’s, moving in for a day or more.
Up until about 15 minutes before the play ends, this is a feel-good comedy, peppered with potent bursts of laughter, a celebratory music and dance interlude, and the occasional topical allusion.

cn.t: Critics embrace this vibrant workplace comedy set in a Harlem braiding salon, praising its ensemble cast, humor, and David Zinn's acclaimed set design, though some find the plot overstuffed with subplots and a late tonal shift uneven.

vr.q: The directing, the acting, the design and the writing are just so good. This play, to me, is the complete package.
It's so impressive how captivating the show is despite it being basically just a day in the life kind of thing.
